strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely problem: the lack of behavioral unification (self-contradiction) in state-of-the-art unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs).

The concept of 'self-contradiction as self-improvement' is elegant and well-executed, leveraging the model's stronger understanding capability to refine its weaker generation branch without external supervision.
The work provides solid theoretical backing by extending the learning dynamics framework (eNTK) to multimodal settings, explaining the mechanisms behind both co-improvement and co-degradation.
The proposed Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) strategy is intuitive and empirically shown to be effective, progressively incorporating harder examples as the model improves.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is primarily centered on the Janus-Pro family (1B and 7B). Testing on other unified architectures like Show-o or Emu3 would demonstrate the broader generalizability of the proposed framework.

The computational overhead associated with the Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) post-training strategy (e.g., the cost of continuously generating candidate images and running evaluations) is not fully analyzed or compared against standard offline methods.

The evaluation relies heavily on T2I-CompBench. Including more comprehensive MLLM benchmarks (such as GenEval for generation and MME/MMBench for understanding) would further validate whether the improvements generalize to broader multimodal tasks.

strengths: Novel and intuitive perspective: Investigating the 'self-contradiction' phenomenon in unified MLLMs and leveraging the asymmetry (stronger understanding vs. weaker generation) for reward-free self-improvement is an elegant and timely idea.

Deep theoretical and empirical analysis of training dynamics: The paper provides a solid theoretical framework (Proposition 1) extending learning dynamics to multimodal tasks, explaining the co-improvement/co-degradation between generation and understanding. This is backed up with rigorous empirical analysis of proxy and direct probability changes.

Crucial caveats identified (Co-degradation): Highlighting that low-quality data can lead to co-degradation and demonstrating that internal metrics like the Nonunified score cannot distinguish it from co-improvement is a valuable and highly practical finding for the community.

Well-designed and effective method: The Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) strategy is highly logical, leveraging the newly active training samples dynamically, and demonstrates consistent gains on both ID and OOD splits.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single model family: The empirical results are exclusively demonstrated on the Janus-Pro family (Janus-Pro-1B and 7B). To demonstrate the generalizability of 'self-contradiction as self-improvement' for unified MLLMs, testing on other architectures (e.g., Show-o, Emu3, or Chameleon) would be highly beneficial.

Small-scale training set: The post-training experiments use a relatively small set of prompts (700 samples from T2I-CompBench 3D Spatial). It is unclear how this self-improvement paradigm scales when applied to larger, more diverse datasets.

Simplified theoretical assumptions: The theoretical model simplifies the prompt and image sequences to single tokens (L=1) and assumes a uniform prior for Bayes' rule derivation. Real MLLM token dynamics might have more complex causal dependencies.

Heavy reliance on a single external judge: The evaluation of understanding improvement and ground truth labels relies strongly on Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct. Relying on a single external judge may introduce model-specific evaluation biases. Additional automated or human evaluation would strengthen the results.

strengths: Highly novel and timely study on self-contradiction and self-improvement in unified Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), focusing on the synchronization between generation and understanding.

Strong theoretical grounding that extends the neural tangent kernel (eNTK) learning dynamics framework to multimodal models, mathematically explaining why SFT/DPO on the generation branch also updates the understanding branch.

Important discovery of the 'co-degradation' risk, where low-quality or corrupted data ruins both branches while misleadingly showing better 'unification' scores, highlighting a critical failure mode of intrinsic self-correction metrics.

The proposed Curriculum Learning-based Online (CLO) strategy is intuitive and effective, progressively introducing more complex prompts (from Ideal to Fully Chosen/Rejected sets) as the model's capabilities evolve.
Excellent writing quality with clear takeaways, intuitive figures, and well-structured empirical analyses.
weaknesses: The evaluation is primarily restricted to the Janus-Pro architecture. Demonstrating these phenomena on other unified MLLMs (e.g., Show-o, Chameleon, or Emu3) would confirm that self-contradiction and co-improvement are universal properties of unified autoregressive models.

The empirical benchmarks are centered around compositional text-to-image tasks (T2I-CompBench). Broader evaluation on standard multimodal understanding benchmarks (e.g., MME, MMBench) and general text-to-image benchmarks (e.g., GenEval) would help guarantee that the self-improvement does not cause regression on other tasks.

The computational overhead and efficiency of the online curriculum generation (CLO) are not thoroughly analyzed in the main text, leaving it unclear how much additional compute is required for the iterative generation and filtering steps.

strengths: Comprehensive and Systematic Analysis: The paper does an excellent job of first quantifying and verifying the internal gap between generation and understanding across six representative unified MLLMs using a newly proposed, self-consistent 'non-unification score'.

Self-Improvement without External Signals: The proposed self-improvement framework is elegant as it leverages the model's own stronger understanding branch to bootstrap its generation capability, avoiding the need for external, heavy reward models.

Deep Theoretical Explanation: Rather than just showing empirical results, the authors investigate and explain the 'co-improvement effect' by extending learning dynamics (eNTK) theory to the multimodal early-fusion setting, showing how joint optimization of generation aligns the learning dynamics of both branches.

Curriculum Learning Integration: The curriculum-based extension (C-SFT) dynamically re-evaluates and expands the post-training dataset, showing a smart way to reclaim previously discarded samples as the model's capabilities evolve.

Strong Empirical Results: Extensive validation on standard benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, Science-T2I) shows that this approach consistently improves both generation and understanding, often surpassing baselines that use external reward models.
weaknesses: Evaluation Scope: While the paper analyzes several MLLMs in its initial verification phase, the actual post-training/self-improvement experiments are only demonstrated on Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o. Extending this to a wider set of unified MLLMs (e.g., BAGEL or EMU3) would strengthen the generalizability claims.

Robustness of Binary Scoring: The calculation of the non-unification score and self-improvement data construction relies on prompting the model's understanding branch to yield binary decisions (0 or 1). Parsing natural language answers from chat models into clean binary signals can sometimes be noisy or highly sensitive to prompt formatting; further analysis of this robustness would be helpful.

Oracle Dependency for 'Weak Generation' metric: The identification of the source of non-unification (attributing it to weak generation) relies on Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct as an external oracle. Although human verification shows good alignment on easy and medium tasks, the discrepancy on hard tasks suggests that the oracle itself has limitations, which could slightly skew the 'Weak Generation' analysis on difficult concepts.

strengths: Widespread empirical validation of the 'internal gap' between generation and understanding across six representative unified MLLMs (EMU3, Show-o, VILA-U, Janus-Pro, BAGEL, BLIP3-o) and diverse difficulty-stratified tasks.

Proposes a completely self-contained self-improvement framework (without external reward models or APIs) that effectively leverages the model's stronger understanding capability to refine its generation capability.

Provides a novel theoretical explanation for the 'co-improvement effect' (where generation tuning also improves understanding) by extending learning dynamics and empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) analysis to unified MLLMs.

Consistently strong experimental results on multiple competitive benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, Science-T2I) and comprehensive ablation studies (e.g., showing that LLM-only tuning is sufficient and validating curriculum learning parameters).
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation of the learning dynamics assumes a shared tokenizer and causal-masking MLLM architecture. While the authors state that the conclusions extend to decoupled architectures (like Janus-Pro), a more formal discussion or verification of how decoupled tokenizers affect the shared eNTK would strengthen the theoretical contribution.

The self-improvement pipeline relies on a starting pool of task-specific prompts (e.g., from T2I-CompBench++). The paper would benefit from discussing how the framework generalizes to open-domain, uncurated, or noisy prompt distributions.

The 'win rate' metric used to evaluate understanding is highly dependent on an external oracle (Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct). Although human evaluation shows high correlation with Qwen, the sensitivity of this metric to the choice of different LLM judges (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is not thoroughly explored.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely topic: the unification and internal performance gap between generation and understanding in unified Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
The proposed 'non-unification score' is an intuitive metric to evaluate the internal consistency of an MLLM's generation and understanding branches without relying on external evaluators.
The proposed gap-based self-improvement framework is elegant and simple, requiring no external reward models or human annotations by leveraging the model's own understanding branch as a critic.
The inclusion of a curriculum learning strategy (C-SFT/C-DPO) to dynamically expand the post-training data by reusing previously discarded prompts is a clever and effective extension.
weaknesses: Fundamental Theoretical Flaw in Section 5 and Appendix E: The core theoretical explanation of the 'co-improvement effect' relies on the assumption in Equation 7 that Bayes' rule holds for the parameterized conditional probabilities of the MLLM, i.e., $\log \pi_\theta(y_0 | x_0) = \log \pi_\theta(x_0 | y_0) - \log \pi_\theta(x_0) + C$. However, in autoregressive MLLMs, $\pi_\theta(y | x)$ (understanding, where text follows image) and $\pi_\theta(x | y)$ (generation, where image follows text) are modeled as two separate conditional autoregressive processes with different causal orderings and prompts. There is no mathematical constraint enforcing that they are consistent with a single joint distribution $\pi_\theta(x, y)$. Therefore, Bayes' relation does not hold for the model's outputs, rendering the subsequent derivations (including Propositions 1 and 2) technically invalid.

Reliability of the Self-Labeling Critic (High False Positives): Figure 6 reveals that approximately 80% of the understanding gains after self-improvement come from correcting false positives (where the pre-trained model incorrectly judged misaligned images as aligned). This implies that the pre-trained model's understanding branch is highly unreliable during the initial SFT/DPO data construction phase. If the critic has a high false-positive rate, the curated 'chosen' data used for self-improvement will inevitably contain many low-quality, misaligned images. The paper lacks a detailed discussion on how this error propagation affects training stability or leads to the reinforcement of the model's own errors/hallucinations.

Marginal Gains on Standard Understanding Benchmarks: While the paper claims a 'co-improvement effect' on understanding, Table 8 shows extremely marginal or sometimes negative performance changes on standard vision-language benchmarks (e.g., POPE drops under SFT/C-SFT, and most other improvements are below 0.5%). This suggests that the self-improvement mainly fits the specific formatting of the pairwise validation task rather than genuinely enhancing general multimodal understanding.

Evaluation Scope: The experimental validation is restricted to older or smaller unified MLLMs (Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o). Evaluating the proposed method on a wider range of larger or state-of-the-art unified architectures would make the findings more general and convincing.
